sources.caveat: Use the book's provocations as diagnostics. Short sentences, sentence-per-line layout, and its composition habits are exercises and perspectives, not mandatory output style.

cards.title: Compare plausible attachments without inventing a rigid nearest-noun rule
cards.mechanism: A modifier or pronoun can create a competing reading that distracts from the intended referent. Diagnose the available readings using syntax and supplied discourse context; proximity alone neither proves the referent nor proves an error.
steps: Identify the exact modifier or referring expression and the plausible candidate referents.
Use agreement, construction, discourse focus, and supplied facts to assess those candidates.
Distinguish a genuinely competing reading from a deliberately strained interpretation the intended reader is unlikely to make.
When the supplied context establishes the referent, reposition or name it with minimal disruption; when it does not, do not silently choose one.
Preserve figurative language, metonymy, and viewpoint when they remain intelligible and serve the task.
triggers: A relative clause sits beside a competing noun and supplied context points to another referent.
An introductory phrase or pronoun appears to attach to an unintended participant.
A proposed criticism depends only on the closest noun or a strained literal reading.
exceptions: Pronouns can refer across intervening nouns when grammar and discourse make the referent clear.
Figurative or metonymic language need not describe literally animate subjects.
A recoverable reference can be stylistically effective even when a contrived alternate reading exists.
Do not infer carelessness, ignorance, or lack of control from one construction.

example.before: The camera was damaged; the lamp was intact. Rina asked Omar to return the camera beside the lamp, which was damaged.
example.after: The camera was damaged; the lamp was intact. Rina asked Omar to return the damaged camera beside the lamp.
example.why: The context identifies the damaged object. Naming it removes the competing attachment without inferring a new fact or appealing to a universal nearest-noun rule.

counterexample.text: Mina opened the cabinet. She found a cracked bowl inside it.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The cabinet is the natural referent of it even though bowl is nearer. A nearest-noun-only criticism would manufacture a problem.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis. Synthesizes practical attachment and reference examples. The source's nearest-noun assertion and some intentionally strained literal readings are not adopted as grammatical rules; the method requires contextual plausibility and calibrated findings.
sources.caveat: Use the book's provocations as diagnostics. Short sentences, sentence-per-line layout, and its composition habits are exercises and perspectives, not mandatory output style.

cards.title: Audit a recommended rewrite even when its source is authoritative
cards.mechanism: A teaching example can illuminate a useful operation while its proposed revision changes a quantity, time span, certainty, or attribution. Treat the recommendation as a candidate to test against the supplied wording, not as evidence that every resulting change is safe.
steps: Identify the editorial operation a model example illustrates, separately from its particular wording.
Record the original passage's quantities, timing, scope, negation, attribution, and degree of certainty.
Compare those commitments with both the proposed rewrite and any supporting context.
Keep the useful operation while restoring unsupported losses or additions; ask when a change would require the writer to supply a fact.
For durable examples, create original text and retain a concise source locator rather than reproducing the author's distinctive passage.
triggers: A suggested improvement makes the prose smoother but weakens an exact duration or scope.
An external editorial authority is being used to justify a rewrite without comparing commitments.
A source's example is being generalized into an unconditional editing rule.
exceptions: A user may explicitly authorize approximation, summarization, or changed content; evaluate the candidate against that actual contract.
An example may isolate one technique without claiming to preserve every dimension; that is a limit on transfer, not proof the author is incompetent.
Literary quality cannot be reduced to exact lexical preservation.
Do not copy a distinctive source example into a new work merely to imitate the demonstrated effect.

example.before: The period during which Mara was unable to climb stairs lasted eighteen months.
example.after: Mara was unable to climb stairs for eighteen months.
example.why: The revision gives Mara the subject position while preserving both inability and the exact duration. A smoother version saying only that she struggled for months would alter two commitments.

counterexample.text: Mara struggled to climb stairs for months.
counterexample.why_not_apply: If this is the only supplied sentence, the editor must not restore eighteen months or complete inability from a familiar example. The reference is a method source, not evidence about Mara.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis. Critical operational synthesis: comparison of the source's before/after examples exposes potential changes in exclusivity, duration, and attribution. This fidelity safeguard evaluates transfer of the examples; it is not presented as the author's explicit rule or proof that every source diagnosis is correct.
sources.caveat: Use the book's provocations as diagnostics. Short sentences, sentence-per-line layout, and its composition habits are exercises and perspectives, not mandatory output style.

cards.title: Let a repeated frame expose changing information
cards.mechanism: A repeated grammatical frame can make differences between observations easier to hear. Judge what each repetition contributes before replacing it with synonyms or smoothing the sequence into a summary.
steps: Identify the stable relation and the distinct information occupying each repeated position.
Compare a parallel sequence with a compact inventory when the task allows both; choose by whether separate beats or rapid scanning better serves the passage.
Preserve the observed distinctions, order when meaningful, and degree of certainty. Do not manufacture escalating stakes to justify a repeated pattern.
triggers: A passage substitutes verbs mainly to avoid repetition even though the relation stays the same.
An authorized revision asks for cadence or for contrasting ways to present a set of observations.
exceptions: Different actions need different verbs; grammatical repetition is not a reason to erase their distinctions.
Exact repetition can serve an incantatory or cumulative purpose, but a compact inventory may better serve a directory or caption.
No number of repeated clauses is inherently effective, and parallel form does not prove logical equivalence.

example.before: The east bed holds peas; the west bed accommodates beans; the narrow bed by the wall hosts mint.
example.after: The east bed holds peas. The west bed holds beans. The narrow bed by the wall holds mint.
example.why: The repeated verb lets location and crop carry the differences. Separate sentences give each bed a beat; this is a functional option for the requested cadence, not a claim that the original is ungrammatical.

practice.task: Offer a plain, rhythmic version of this garden inventory and a compact alternative. Keep every location and crop; these are alternative presentations, not a grammar correction.
invariants: Peas are in the east bed and beans in the west bed.
Mint is in the narrow bed by the wall; narrow and by the wall describe that bed.
Do not invent colors, scents, planting order, quantities, or an assertion that these are the only crops.

alternatives.text: East bed: peas. West bed: beans. Narrow bed by the wall: mint.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use for a compact garden label or quickly scanned inventory when fragments are permitted.
alternatives.tradeoff: The layout makes retrieval faster but loses the full sentences' evenly voiced cadence.

counterexample.text: The pump draws water; the valve directs it; the filter traps grit.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The distinct verbs identify different functions. A proofreading task gives no reason to replace them with one generic repeated verb or to recast a clear sequence.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis from literary passages and the commentary distinguishing purposeful invariant structure from automatic variation. The inventory, alternative formats, and factual safeguards are original applications, not borrowed literary sentences or an assertion of one correct authorial intention.
sources.caveat: Use the book's provocations as diagnostics. Short sentences, sentence-per-line layout, and its composition habits are exercises and perspectives, not mandatory output style.

cards.title: Let exact details carry a passage with ordinary verbs
cards.mechanism: A scene can be particular and alive even when its verbs are ordinary. Inspect the supplied objects, relations, and selection of detail before demanding more dramatic verbs or adding sensory material.
steps: List the concrete distinctions already supplied and identify what the passage asks the reader to notice.
Test a neutral verb or an inventory structure against the original phrasing; preserve each object's identity and location.
Keep a strong verb when it states a meaningful action. Reject a vivid replacement that adds movement, attitude, sound, or intention absent from the record.
triggers: A request to enliven prose risks replacing be or other ordinary verbs mechanically.
A scene contains specific supplied objects but their presentation is inflated or generic.
exceptions: This is not a preference for weak verbs: a precise action verb is valuable when an action is actually established.
A plain inventory is not always the desired voice; preserve a deliberate metaphor unless the task authorizes changing it.
Sensory expansion is appropriate only when supplied evidence or explicit fictional invention permission supports it.

example.before: A trio of notices occupies the glass beside the entrance: a room advertisement, a concert announcement, and a lost-dog notice.
example.after: Three notices are on the glass beside the entrance: a room advertisement, a concert announcement, and a lost-dog notice.
example.why: The exact contents already distinguish the scene. Neutral wording lets those details register without pretending that the notices perform a dramatic action.

practice.task: Make this observed description plainer and offer a second arrangement. Preserve all recorded details; do not invent a scene to make it vivid.
invariants: There are three notices on the glass beside the entrance.
The notices comprise a room advertisement, a concert announcement, and a lost-dog notice.
No date, color, fastening method, material condition, observer emotion, or outcome is supplied.

alternatives.text: On the glass beside the entrance are three notices: a room advertisement, a concert announcement, and a lost-dog notice.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when the surrounding description follows locations and the entrance glass is the next place to orient the reader.
alternatives.tradeoff: The location-first structure delays the notices themselves; the main version introduces the objects more promptly.

counterexample.text: The latch snapped and the gate swung open.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The verbs state supplied actions precisely. Replacing them with generic states would remove the movement and sequence; no plain-language rule requires doing so.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis from the literary selection and page-81 attention to passages whose effect is not dependent on elaborate verbs. The original notice example and observation-versus-invention constraints operationalize the question; they do not reproduce the source's scenery or treat its questions as universal rules.
sources.caveat: Use the book's provocations as diagnostics. Short sentences, sentence-per-line layout, and its composition habits are exercises and perspectives, not mandatory output style.

cards.title: Compare frame order without changing a condition's scope
cards.mechanism: Moving a time frame or condition changes where the reader begins without necessarily changing what is asserted. Compare the resulting emphasis while checking that all conditions still govern the same event; an elegant reorder is unsafe if it strengthens an if into an only if.
steps: State the conditions and resulting event separately before changing their order.
Try a context-first form and an integrated conditional form when alternatives are requested.
Compare which information arrives first and what remains implicit. Reject changes that add exclusivity, causality, a deadline, or a claim about cases outside the stated condition.
triggers: A request asks for different sentence perspectives on a conditional event.
Several opening frames are grammatically clear but an alternative order could better orient the reader.
exceptions: An already clear conditional sentence is not defective merely because another order is possible.
Chronology, negation, and qualifier attachment can make seemingly interchangeable frame orders non-equivalent.
Do not infer what happens when the condition is false; the sentence may not establish it.

example.before: On market days, if it rains, the stalls move under the arcade.
example.after: If it rains on a market day, the stalls move under the arcade.
example.why: The revision packages the two conditions together; the original establishes market days as the topic first. Both retain the same supplied rule without claiming the stalls move only in rain.

practice.task: Compare alternative sentence forms for this standing arrangement. The original is already acceptable; preserve its conditions and do not infer what happens on other days.
invariants: Rain on a market day is the supplied condition for moving the stalls under the arcade.
The text does not say whether stalls move on dry days or outside market days.
Do not add a responsible actor, a reason, an exact time, or an only-if restriction.

alternatives.text: On rainy market days, the stalls move under the arcade.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when the audience benefits from a compact recurring-schedule statement and the compound condition is easy to recognize.
alternatives.tradeoff: The phrase is shorter but makes the logical condition less explicit than the if-clause; use the if form when explaining the rule itself matters.

counterexample.text: Only if the hall is full will the overflow room open.
counterexample.why_not_apply: Only if states a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. A rewrite saying If the hall is full, the overflow room will open would add a guarantee. In proofreading, leave the correct original intact.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis prompted by the comparison of alternative orders for ordinary time and conditional clauses. Explicit truth-condition checks, the market example, and the only-if exception are the assistant's safeguards rather than a formal logic method claimed for the source.
sources.caveat: Use the book's provocations as diagnostics. Short sentences, sentence-per-line layout, and its composition habits are exercises and perspectives, not mandatory output style.

cards.title: Let a content clause carry the central information without losing its source
cards.mechanism: A grammatically dependent clause can carry the information that matters most. Its reporting frame may preserve attribution, belief, doubt, or a question; promoting its contents to an independent assertion can silently remove those limits.
steps: Identify both the embedded proposition and the reporting, belief, uncertainty, or questioning frame that governs it.
Distinguish grammatical dependency from informational importance; do not promote a clause merely because its content is central.
Compare an integrated content clause with an independently phrased but explicitly attributed version, preserving the same source and commitment.
Choose the form that gives the requested focus with the least unnecessary repetition; retain uncertainty and attribution in either form.
triggers: A revision proposes to move an important reported claim out of a dependent clause.
A generic reporting sentence duplicates the specific information in the next sentence.
An editor treats grammatical subordination as proof that information is unimportant.
exceptions: A source frame is not automatically expendable throat-clearing; it can be the only distinction between a record and an independently established fact.
Direct assertion can be appropriate when the task and evidence authorize it, but sentence restructuring alone supplies no such authorization.
A dependent clause is not automatically clearer or more artful than an independent one; compare actual focus, scope, and rhythm.

example.before: The logger recorded something. It recorded that the chamber warmed by two degrees after midnight.
example.after: The logger recorded that the chamber warmed by two degrees after midnight.
example.why: The content clause carries the substantive information. Removing the duplicated reporting sentence does not remove the logger as the source of the temperature report.

practice.task: Make this report concise while keeping the temperature change tied to the logger's record, not presented as independently verified.
invariants: The logger is the source of the reported change.
The chamber warmed by two degrees, not to two degrees, in the logger's record.
The reported change occurred after midnight; no cause or independent verification is supplied.

alternatives.text: According to the logger, the chamber warmed by two degrees after midnight.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when the reader needs the temperature event in the main clause but the report's source must remain explicit.
alternatives.tradeoff: The event gains grammatical prominence while the attribution remains a qualifying frame; this is a change of focus, not stronger evidence.

alternatives.text: The chamber warmed by two degrees after midnight, according to the logger.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when the chamber is already the topic and the sentence is read as a whole.
alternatives.tradeoff: The attribution arrives last and can be overlooked in a clipped excerpt; front-load it if attribution is especially consequential.

counterexample.text: No one knows whether the chamber warmed after midnight.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The dependent question is the unresolved issue, not an asserted warming event. Turning it into a bare statement would invent certainty; the sentence does not need correction merely because its important content is dependent.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis. The reviewed discussion separates grammatical dependency from importance and illustrates nominal clauses in statements, questions, dialogue, and reports. The attribution-preservation procedure and all practice sentences are original operational extensions, not quotations.
sources.caveat: Use examples to understand syntactic functions, not to imitate distinctive prose. No construction is automatically desirable outside its context.

cards.title: Reduce stacked relative clauses without changing which thing is meant
cards.mechanism: A relative clause can identify its noun, supply extra information, or extend a sentence's texture. Several embedded relatives can delay the main action. Compressing or moving them helps only if the same referent and qualifying relations survive.
steps: Recover the base assertion and map each relative clause to the noun it qualifies.
Determine which details identify a particular referent and which merely add information; do not infer exclusivity or a larger population without support.
Compare the original embedding with a compact phrase or a rearranged main clause, keeping every identification and the scope of each qualifier.
Check that added commas, clause splitting, or omitted qualifiers have not broadened the claim to every member of a group.
triggers: A relative clause contains another relative clause and postpones the predicate readers need.
A proposed simplification drops the detail distinguishing one permit, object, person, or subset from another.
A punctuation change would turn selecting information into a supplementary assertion.
exceptions: A short relative clause can be the clearest identification and needs no compression.
Nested clauses can remain legible and create deliberate accumulation or suspense; nesting is not itself a defect.
A reduced phrase can introduce ambiguity, tense loss, or an unsupported relation. Reject it if it does not preserve the original commitments.

example.before: The permit that covers the loading bay that faces the canal expires on Monday.
example.after: The permit for the canal-facing loading bay expires on Monday.
example.why: The compact modifier preserves which loading bay the permit covers and lets the expiry claim arrive sooner. It does not imply that every permit expires or that there is only one loading bay.

practice.task: Make the permit notice easier to scan while preserving which loading bay is covered and when the permit expires.
invariants: The relevant permit covers the loading bay facing the canal.
That permit expires on Monday.
The text supplies no count of permits or loading bays and no claim about any other permit.

alternatives.text: The permit for the loading bay facing the canal expires on Monday.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when a compound adjective would be less familiar than an ordinary descriptive phrase.
alternatives.tradeoff: This is slightly longer than the compact revision, but it reduces one level of embedding without changing the notice's emphasis.

alternatives.text: On Monday, the permit for the loading bay facing the canal expires.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use in a date-led schedule where the expiry day is the reader's first sorting need.
alternatives.tradeoff: The identifying bay detail arrives later; retain the original topic-first order if several permits are being contrasted.

counterexample.text: The samples that failed the heat test were discarded.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The brief relative clause defines the affected samples. Removing it, or automatically setting it off with commas, can turn a subset claim into a claim about all samples. No cumbersome embedding requires repair.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis. The reviewed pages discuss relative-clause placement, bound and free modification, successful embedding, and a long embedding that delays its main point. The subset-scope checks and original permit examples operationalize those distinctions; they are not reproductions of the literary examples.
sources.caveat: Use examples to understand syntactic functions, not to imitate distinctive prose. No construction is automatically desirable outside its context.

cards.title: Use a nominal clause to put the specific open question in focus
cards.mechanism: A clause beginning with who, what, how, or a similar word can name the matter a sentence addresses. This can turn a vague abstract label into a precise question or contrast. Its rhetorical neatness does not establish the answer or justify a general maxim.
steps: Identify the exact known event and the distinct information that remains unknown or under discussion.
Try a nominal clause that names that open question directly, retaining the supplied certainty and uncertainty.
Compare a clause-based version with a plain noun-based version; choose for the reader's immediate question and the sentence's rhythm.
Do not manufacture an answer, an aphoristic generalization, or a contrast unsupported by the supplied material.
triggers: An abstract phrase obscures whether the uncertainty concerns who, what, how, or why.
A sentence needs to distinguish an established event from a specific unanswered question.
A polished nominal-clause pattern seems to imply more general knowledge than the evidence provides.
exceptions: A direct noun phrase may be shorter and equally precise; do not add a what-clause simply to sound reflective.
Known information should not be converted into a mystery for dramatic effect.
An elegant contrast, aphorism, or balanced pair is not evidence that its claim is true.

example.before: The final parcel was delivered. The identity of the person who received it is unknown.
example.after: The final parcel was delivered, but who received it is unknown.
example.why: The nominal clause names the precise gap in knowledge. Delivery remains established, and the missing identity is not converted into a suspicion about whether delivery occurred.

practice.task: Combine the status note into one clear sentence that distinguishes the known delivery from the unknown recipient; do not invent an identity or explanation.
invariants: The final parcel was delivered.
The recipient's identity is unknown in this account.
No delivery time, cause of the missing information, or suspect is supplied.

alternatives.text: The final parcel was delivered; its recipient is unknown.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use for a compact operational note where recipient is familiar and the two status facts deserve equal weight.
alternatives.tradeoff: The noun-based version is more compressed and less explicitly question-shaped; it is not inferior simply because it lacks a nominal clause.

alternatives.text: Who received the final parcel is unknown, but the parcel was delivered.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when responding first to a question about identity and then confirming delivery.
alternatives.tradeoff: This reverses the informational emphasis without reversing the facts; it is less suited to a delivery-first status list.

counterexample.text: The final parcel reached Dana at noon.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The recipient and time are supplied. Inventing an open question or padding the sentence with a what-clause would weaken an already direct report.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis. The nominal-clause discussion connects these forms with implicit questions, expansion, dialogue, and aphoristic effects, then warns that they can become pretentious. The known-versus-unknown exercise and non-invention checks are original applications, not copied sentences or universal grammatical rules.
sources.caveat: Use examples to understand syntactic functions, not to imitate distinctive prose. No construction is automatically desirable outside its context.

cards.title: Prepare a later use with an already established detail
cards.mechanism: A detail that first appears at the moment it solves a story problem can feel retrofitted. If the supplied material already establishes it, an authorized reorder can make the later use intelligible without manufacturing a clue.
steps: Locate the later use and the earlier source material establishing possession, existence, or capability.
Check whether advance orientation serves this story or would spoil an intended revelation.
When restructuring is authorized, introduce the supplied detail earlier without inventing acquisition, intent, or new foreshadowing.
Compare a separate setup sentence with a detail integrated into the existing scene; keep the payoff and the factual timeline intact.
triggers: A supplied object or capability appears only as it resolves a difficulty.
The user authorizes restructuring to prepare a later event using existing material.
exceptions: A mystery may intentionally reveal the means late; preparation is not compulsory explanation.
Do not invent a clue, capability, memory, or acquisition event to make a payoff seem earned.
A proofreading or local-edit request does not authorize cross-scene reordering.
A mentioned object need not have a later payoff; a craft maxim is not a universal law.

example.before: At the old pumping station, Lio found the inspection hatch sealed. He released it with the flat steel key he had been carrying since morning. He went down the ladder.
example.after: Lio had been carrying the flat steel key since morning. At the old pumping station, he found the inspection hatch sealed, released it with the key, and went down the ladder.
example.why: The key is available to the reader before its use. Its prior possession, material, the sealed hatch, and the descent remain established facts; no reason for carrying it is invented.

practice.task: Restructure this fictional passage to establish the key before the sealed hatch is encountered. Preserve every supplied fact; do not invent how or why Lio obtained the key.
invariants: Lio has carried a flat steel key since morning.
The inspection hatch at the old pumping station is sealed before Lio releases it with that key.
Lio then goes down the ladder; no acquisition event or motive is supplied.

alternatives.text: Lio had been carrying a key since morning, a flat steel key. At the old pumping station, he found the inspection hatch sealed. He released it with the key and went down the ladder.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when the setup should register distinctly before the obstacle, with a separate beat for the sealed hatch.
alternatives.tradeoff: Repetition gives the key more emphasis and costs words; it would be excessive if the story needs an unobtrusive setup.

counterexample.text: Lio lifted the coat lining. A key was stitched inside. Until then, neither Lio nor the reader knew it was there.
counterexample.why_not_apply: A task preserving this discovery does not permit introducing the key into Lio's earlier knowledge. A late revelation can be intentional; inventing prior awareness would change the scene.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis: The commentary's fifth keyed revision brings an existing later prop forward. The assistant-specific constraint is to use only supplied detail under explicit restructuring authority, not to import the author's freedom to invent or a universal payoff rule.
sources.caveat: Treat the book's vivid cautions and personal working process as craft heuristics, not universal prohibitions or a mandatory drafting schedule.

cards.title: Retain a delivery cue when it changes how dialogue is understood
cards.mechanism: The literal wording of a line may not establish whether it is sincere, mocking, reluctant, or performed. A supplied delivery cue can carry that distinction; remove duplicate explanation without deleting the cue that prevents a different reading.
steps: Identify what the quoted words establish and what the supplied delivery description adds.
Do not infer mockery or another mental state merely because the surrounding event makes it plausible.
Compare a compact attribution with a separate explicit framing clause using the same supported delivery.
Remove only duplicated explanation; preserve exact dialogue, speaker, event, and the intended speech act.
triggers: A blanket adverb cut would make explicitly sarcastic praise read as potentially sincere.
The same supplied delivery is explained twice around a line of dialogue.
exceptions: When the line or surrounding material already supplies the delivery sufficiently, a tag may be unnecessary.
A surprising contrast does not prove sarcasm, deception, or a motive.
Do not replace a delivery cue with an invented smile, gesture, tone of voice, or interior thought.
Reported dialogue and quotations remain source-bound even if a fictional exercise elsewhere permits invention.

example.before: The replacement arrived broken. 'Excellent work,' Sera said sarcastically, making a sarcastic comment.
example.after: The replacement arrived broken. 'Excellent work,' Sera said sarcastically.
example.why: The duplicate explanation disappears, but the supplied sarcastic delivery remains. Removing all delivery information would not preserve the same explicit distinction between mockery and literal praise.

practice.task: Remove the redundant delivery explanation. Preserve the broken replacement, Sera as speaker, the exact words of her line, and her explicitly sarcastic delivery. Do not add an action or motive.
invariants: The replacement arrives broken.
Sera says 'Excellent work' sarcastically.
No cause of the breakage, gesture, or motive is supplied.

alternatives.text: The replacement arrived broken. Sera was being sarcastic when she said, 'Excellent work.'
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when the reader should know the delivery before encountering the apparently positive words.
alternatives.tradeoff: The explanatory frame is longer and places more emphasis on the delivery than the compact attribution.

counterexample.text: The replacement arrived broken. 'Excellent work,' Sera said sincerely. She was praising the repair team for finding a separate fault.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The source explicitly establishes sincere praise and its target. Do not impose sarcasm because a similar example used it or because the broken replacement makes sarcasm seem likely.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis: The eighth keyed revision retains a dialogue adverb to convey a nonliteral interpersonal effect. This supports contextual selection, not a ban or quota. The original exercise states sarcasm explicitly rather than treating an adverb alone as proof of intent.
sources.caveat: Treat the book's vivid cautions and personal working process as craft heuristics, not universal prohibitions or a mandatory drafting schedule.

cards.title: Compress routine handling without deleting consequential staging
cards.mechanism: Narration can spell out predictable handling steps that contribute little, but position, contact, access, and sequence sometimes explain the action. Test a cut against the scene state, not against a general dislike of stage direction.
steps: Track the actor's established position and the object, contact, access, and movement involved.
Identify which handling steps the current task permits compressing and which facts make the event possible or distinctive.
Compare a compact action with a slightly more explicit sequence, retaining all task-required commitments.
Recheck the result for changed posture, means, agency, order, or physical access; retain extra detail when it performs that work.
triggers: A local narrative request allows routine reach-and-grasp scaffolding to be compressed.
Cutting an action beat risks removing the spatial relation or means the next action depends on.
exceptions: A forensic account, technical sequence, choreography, or accessibility detail may require the exact mechanics.
An ordinary expectation is not evidence that a character used a hand, sat in a chair, or could reach an object.
Do not delete movements that establish suspense, hesitation, characterization, or later constraints.
Do not apply the author's percentage-cut heuristic as a mandatory target.

example.before: Ira was already standing at the open hatch. She reached out with her hand, took hold of the handle, and pulled the hatch shut.
example.after: Already standing at the open hatch, Ira pulled it shut by the handle.
example.why: For a request that permits compressing routine handling, the shortened sentence retains the initial standing position, open hatch, closing action, and handle. It does not invent a different means of closing it.

practice.task: Compress routine reach-and-grasp staging. Keep Ira's initial standing position at the open hatch, her use of the handle, and the closing action. You may omit the ordinary hand-reaching step.
invariants: Ira is already standing at the open hatch.
Ira uses its handle to pull the hatch shut.
The task permits omission of the routine reach; it does not permit a changed location or means.

alternatives.text: Ira was already standing at the open hatch. She took the handle and pulled it shut.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Use when separate setup and action beats suit the scene better than folding the setup into a modifier.
alternatives.tradeoff: It is less compressed but keeps the grasp visible and gives the action a separate sentence.

counterexample.text: Ira kept both feet behind the chalk line and used a hook to pull the hatch shut.
counterexample.why_not_apply: The position and tool are distinctive constraints. A revision saying only that she shut the hatch would lose them; replacing the hook with her hand would invent a different action.

sources.note: Source-grounded application synthesis: The fourth and sixth keyed revisions cut routine staging. The application adds an explicit scene-invariant check and rejects treating ordinary expectations about seating or movement as universal fact.
sources.caveat: Treat the book's vivid cautions and personal working process as craft heuristics, not universal prohibitions or a mandatory drafting schedule.
